## The main branch's CI after a merge, required checks, and an owner-word wake routine that works from its brief

### The main branch's CI is read after every merge (#88)

In an adopting app four of five merges ended with a red `ci` run on the main branch while every pull request had been
green, and nobody noticed for a day. One failure had been recorded as "a timing failure, unrelated"; it was a real bug.

- **`softure-worktree/scripts/wt-main-ci.py [<sha>]`** reads the push-triggered GitHub Actions runs on a commit (the
  merge, or `origin/<main>`'s head) through `gh` and prints `MAIN-CI green | red | flaky | running | none |
  superseded`. A run that passed only on a re-run is `flaky` (exit 1, like `red`).
- **Threads** (`rules/AGENTS.md`, `softure-worktree` Phase B) read the main branch's CI on their merge commit after
  `wt-roadmap.py done`, report it, and close only when it is green. A red or flaky merge is the thread's to fix, as a
  new change.
- **The heartbeat** (`routines/roadmap-heartbeat.md`) sends `main CI: <verdict>` on every fire; the coordinator puts it
  into the report (`CI on <main>: green`) and starts a fix thread when it is red or flaky and nobody fixes it.
- **Managed block:** a test that fails once and passes on a re-run is a bug, never a timing failure.
- **`doctor --protection`** (`ci_config.py --protection`) asks the forge whether the main branch requires every
  pull-request CI job as a status check, administrators included (classic protection or a ruleset):
  `FAIL main-checks-not-required` per gap, exit 75 when the token cannot tell. `softure-init` runs it and lists each
  gap as an owner step.

### Owner-word wake: a brief that creates a working routine by itself (#95)

In an adopting portfolio eleven wake routines never fired: their GitHub trigger was first saved as
`Pull request: Opened` and switched to `Issue: Opened` later, which the form shows but the trigger never applies, and
the web form had attached every connector of the account.

- **The setup brief** (`routines/owner-word-wake.md`) creates the GitHub trigger in the same call that creates the
  task: `Issue: Opened`, filtered on the wake label, no connectors, a fresh session per fire. It reads the task back
  (deletes it when the stored trigger or connectors differ), opens a labelled test issue, waits for the claim, and only
  then sets `autonomy.ownerWordWake` to `"routine"`. To change an existing trigger's event: delete it, save, add a
  new one, save.
- **`autonomy.ownerWordWakeLabel`** (default `"cockpit"`, the label COCKPIT adds next to `owner-word`; a project
  without COCKPIT sets `"owner-word"`) is the label the trigger filters on; the routine treats an issue with it as an
  owner-word issue and still acts only on authors who can write to the repository. The task is named
  `<PROJECT> · COCKPIT command` (`<PROJECT> · Owner-word wake` with `"owner-word"`).
- **Doctor:** `owner-word-wake-invalid` also covers a wake label that is not one label name; `doctor --protection`
  fails with `owner-word-wake-label-missing` when the routine is declared and `owner-word` or the wake label does not
  exist.

Adopting apps with a wake routine: delete the old task and run the new brief once; it opens the test issue itself.
